To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the EEG is not useful to distinguish between stroke mimics, stroke chameleones, and other causes of TND; 2) non specific focal slowing is the most common EEG pattern in TND; 3) epileptiform activity is uncommon in TND, but may be found in patients with focal seizure and migraine aura.
the EEG is abnormal in 42% of patients with transient neurologic deficit, and is not helpful to distinguish between ischemic and other causes.
EEG is not useful for diagnosis of transient neurological deficits.

the EEG in transient ischemic attack (TIA) and other transient neurological symptoms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EEG is of limited value in TND.

a normal EEG does not rule out a stroke, and that an abnormal EEG is not a stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EEG is useful to rule out focal seizure and migraine aura in TND, but is not useful to identify stroke mimics or stroke chameleon.
EEG is not a reliable tool for the diagnosis of stroke mimics.

, in the case of a TND, EEG is useful to rule out focal seizure and migraine aura, but not to identify stroke mimics or stroke chameleon, which should be identified by the clinical presentation, the brain imaging study, and the clinical course.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EEG should be considered early, within 7 day of TND onset, and should be performed by a trained neurologist.
EEG is not helpful for identifying stroke mimics and chameleons.
